lineage_context.teaching_goal: Use the small hypanthium/disc flower with stamens opposite the petals as the family-level door, then split local genera by armature, venation and fruit type.

project_scope.selection_mode: Central Texas family-first module across six source-pool genera / five current accepted genus concepts
project_scope.note: The raw pool carries Ziziphus obtusifolia and Condaliopsis obtusifolia as separate source concepts. Current Kew treats Z. obtusifolia as a synonym of Condaliopsis obtusifolia, so the legacy name is retained only as provenance.

family_diagnostics.where_to_look_first: Do not start with thorns. Start with a small 4–5-part flower and look for a conspicuous nectar disc/hypanthium with the stamens positioned opposite the petals. Then use fruit architecture—drupe versus capsule—and stipules/armature to enter the genus.
family_diagnostics.vegetative: Mostly shrubs or small trees in the local pool. Leaves are simple, usually alternate, with stipules; stipules may become spines in some genera. Venation may be pinnate or strongly 3-veined from near the base.
family_diagnostics.reproductive: Flowers are usually small and radial, commonly 4–5-merous. Petals may be tiny or absent. A nectar disc is usually conspicuous, and the stamens are antipetalous—opposite the petals rather than alternating with them.
family_diagnostics.fruit: Highly useful but variable: local genera include dry capsules and fleshy drupes. Ovary position also varies across the family, so fruit + genus architecture is safer than an ovary-position absolute.
family_diagnostics.field_tip: The unusual clue is stamens opposite the petals. Pair that with a disc/hypanthium and a one-seed-per-locule fruit plan; then decide capsule or drupe.

visual_lesson.teaching_order: small disc flower → stamens opposite petals → stipule/thorn + venation → capsule-vs-drupe → genus doors → Rosales comparison
visual_lesson.intro: Buckthorns are easy to miss because the flowers are tiny. The flower geometry is the giveaway: a conspicuous disc and stamens sitting directly in front of the petals.

steps.title: 1 · Find the floral disc
steps.look_for: Tiny 4–5-part flower with a broad nectar disc filling or lining the floral cup.
steps.why_it_matters: The disc is a repeatable Rhamnaceae clue when the shrub itself looks generic.

steps.title: 2 · Check where the stamens sit
steps.look_for: Stamens opposite the petals, often tucked against small hooded petals.
steps.why_it_matters: Antipetalous stamens are one of the best family-level confirmation characters.

steps.title: 3 · Read the node and basal veins
steps.look_for: Simple leaf, stipule or stipular spine when present, and either pinnate or strong basal 3-vein architecture.
steps.why_it_matters: This routes the plant toward Colubrina, thorny condalia/lotebush doors, Frangula or Ceanothus.

steps.title: 4 · Split capsule from drupe
steps.look_for: Colubrina/Ceanothus-type dry fruits versus fleshy one- or several-stoned drupes in Condalia, Condaliopsis and Frangula.
steps.why_it_matters: Fruit is the fastest local genus sorter once family is known.

steps.title: 5 · Colubrina door: 3-veined + capsule
steps.look_for: Unarmed shrub, leaves strongly 3-veined from near the base, and a dry capsular fruit.
steps.why_it_matters: Separates Texas snakewood from the thorny drupe-bearing local doors.

steps.title: 6 · Condalia / Condaliopsis door: thorny + drupe
steps.look_for: Thorny shrub architecture and small fleshy drupes; use accepted genus/taxonomy rather than old lotebush names alone.
steps.why_it_matters: These are likely field confusions in dry Central Texas shrubland.

steps.title: 7 · Frangula and Ceanothus exceptions
steps.look_for: Frangula is unarmed and drupe-bearing; Ceanothus tends toward showier clustered flowers and a dry lobed capsule.
steps.why_it_matters: Prevents 'thorny buckthorn' from becoming a false family rule.

comparisons.title: Rhamnaceae vs Rosaceae
comparisons.rule: Both can be woody with 5-part flowers, but Rhamnaceae commonly has a strong nectar disc and stamens opposite the petals; Rosaceae usually has stamens alternating with petals and often many stamens.

comparisons.title: Rhamnaceae vs Cannabaceae/Ulmaceae
comparisons.rule: Celtis and Ulmus are recognized more readily by leaf venation plus drupe/samara. Rhamnaceae confirmation comes from the disc flower with antipetalous stamens and family-specific capsule/drupe doors.

comparisons.title: Rhamnaceae vs Moraceae
comparisons.rule: Local Moraceae has milky latex, minute unisexual inflorescences and multiple fruits; Rhamnaceae lacks the mulberry/Osage-orange multiple-fruit plan and uses the small disc flower.

visual_lesson.caveat: Rhamnaceae varies in leaf arrangement, ovary position, petals and fruit type. Never teach thorns, alternate leaves or drupes as universal; the disc + antipetalous-stamen clue is the better family anchor.

anatomy_examples.plain_label: Stamens face petals around nectar disc
anatomy_examples.photo_role: Exact-species front and oblique flower macro; matched Schaefferia cuneifolia reproductive flower at same scale
anatomy_examples.look_for: Magnify a correctly identified flower from the face and side. Locate the nectar disc and floral cup, then check stamen position only where individual petals are actually visible. Do not infer opposite stamens from petal-less flowers.
anatomy_examples.caption: Inspect the tiny flower's disc and cup; only call stamens antipetalous when the petals are visible.

anatomy_examples.plain_label: Three strong basal veins and dry splitting fruit
anatomy_examples.photo_role: Exact-species leaf underside and opened capsule; matched Celtis leaf and drupe
anatomy_examples.look_for: Trace the three major veins from near the leaf base on a correctly identified Texas snakewood, then compare an intact and opened ripe dry capsule. A Celtis leaf can share the vein pattern; compare its fleshy drupe.
anatomy_examples.caption: Three basal veins suggest Colubrina, but the dry capsule is the useful tie-breaker against a similarly veined Celtis.

family_confusion_polish.look_here_first: Find the nectar disc in a small flower and check for stamens opposite petals; then confirm fruit type. Thorns, basal three-vein leaves and drupes alone are not proof.
separators: Rosaceae: compare petal-to-stamen placement, stamen number, hypanthium and fruit.
Celtis/Cannabaceae: compare a Colubrina dry capsule with a Celtis one-stoned drupe; basal leaf veins overlap.
Ulmaceae: contrast flat winged Ulmus samaras with Rhamnaceae drupes or capsules.
Sapindaceae: check opposite/compound leaf nodes and paired samaras rather than a generic woody habit.
genus_doors: Colubrina: basal-three-veined leaves plus dry capsule.
Condalia/Condaliopsis: thorny short shoots plus drupes; confirm current key; Ziziphus source name is alias only.
Ceanothus: clustered flowers and dry lobed capsule.
